batchName: Late Republic: Cicero, Catiline and the Triumvirate (63-53 BCE) - Easy Batch 2
chapterName: Late Republic: Cicero, Catiline and the Triumvirate (63-53 BCE)

questions.question: Almost everything we know about Catiline comes from whom?
questions.explanation: Our picture of Catiline comes almost entirely from hostile sources. The first is Cicero, the very consul who crushed the plot.
questions.sourceQuote: Almost everything we know about Catiline comes from his enemies.

questions.question: What is the scholarly consensus on Catiline's conspiracy?
options: It was real but its danger was exaggerated
It was invented entirely by Cicero
It came close to overthrowing the government
It was secretly directed by Caesar
questions.explanation: Most scholars accept that the plot was real but believe its danger was overstated. Theories that Cicero invented it, or that Caesar or Crassus pulled the strings, are rejected.
questions.sourceQuote: The consensus is that the plot was real, but its danger was exaggerated.

questions.question: What title did senators give Cicero after the conspirators were executed?
questions.explanation: Senators hailed Cicero as "pater patriae", father of the fatherland. The glory soon soured, as enemies later attacked him for killing citizens without trial.
questions.sourceQuote: Senators hailed him as "father of the fatherland" (*pater patriae*).

questions.question: Which power did Crassus attack in search of military glory?
questions.explanation: Crassus targeted the Parthian Empire, which ruled Iran and Mesopotamia. Critics objected that Parthia had given Rome no reason for war.
questions.sourceQuote: His target was the Parthian Empire, a power ruling Iran and Mesopotamia.

questions.question: What did Caesar give up in 60 BC so he could stand for consul?
options: His command of legions in Gaul
questions.explanation: Caesar sacrificed a triumph, the grand parade every general craved, in order to run for the consulship. His enemies then saddled him with a hostile fellow consul.
questions.sourceQuote: Caesar, back from governing southern Spain, gave up a triumph (*triumphus*), the grand victory parade every general craved, so he could stand for consul.

questions.question: Which office did Catiline repeatedly stand for, only to be rejected by the voters every time?
questions.explanation: Catiline kept losing elections for the consulship, Rome's top office, shared each year by two consuls. After yet another defeat in autumn 63 BC, he turned to force.
questions.sourceQuote: Catiline had stood for it repeatedly and been rejected by the voters every time.

questions.question: After Catiline left Rome to join the rebels, what did the Senate declare him?
questions.explanation: The Senate branded Catiline a public enemy and sent Cicero's fellow consul to fight him. He had left the city after Cicero denounced him to his face.
questions.sourceQuote: The Senate declared him a public enemy (*hostis*) and sent Cicero's fellow consul to fight him.

questions.question: What did Pompey promise if anyone raised a sword against Caesar's land law?
options: He would call up his legions
questions.explanation: Pompey's sword-and-shield remark revealed the secret alliance behind Caesar's law. The fellow consul had insisted the people would not get the law that year even if they all wanted it.
questions.sourceQuote: Pompey said that if anyone raised a sword against the law, he would bring a shield.

questions.question: What is true of the name "First Triumvirate"?
options: It was the trio's official title
No ancient writer ever used it
Cicero coined it in a speech
The Senate granted it in 59 BC
questions.explanation: No ancient writer called the alliance a triumvirate, and it was never an official post. Many modern historians now avoid the term as misleading.
questions.sourceQuote: But no ancient writer called it that, and it was never an official post.

questions.question: Where did Caesar meet Pompey in 56 BC to renew their alliance?
questions.explanation: Caesar met Pompey at Luca, modern Lucca, then the southernmost town of his province. He met Crassus separately at Ravenna.
questions.sourceQuote: Caesar met Crassus at Ravenna and Pompey at Luca, modern Lucca, then the southernmost town of Caesar's province in northern Italy.
